opus-5.5.text:
I think part of why existential risk has such public appeal is that it's a very clean story. It has a clear villain, it has enormous stakes, and it lets people project whatever anxieties they have about technology onto a single, dramatic endpoint. It's also, frankly, a story that's quite comfortable for the people building these systems, because it centers the technology as extraordinarily powerful and it positions a small group of labs as the ones who need to steward it.

But when I think about how these models are actually going to be used around the world, the framing starts to feel very narrow. Most people will encounter AI not as some runaway superintelligence, but as a chatbot answering a health question in Yoruba, or a model screening loan applications, or a content moderation system deciding what gets taken down in a language it was barely trained on. And the risks there are very concrete and very present. Models that perform dramatically worse outside of English. Safety guardrails that simply don't hold up when you prompt in a lower-resource language. Systems that encode a particular cultural lens and then get deployed globally as if that lens were neutral.

So my concern isn't that we should never think about long-term risk. Researchers should be able to think about a wide range of failure modes. My concern is about allocation, about where attention, funding, and policy energy go. If the dominant public conversation is about a hypothetical future catastrophe, it can crowd out the harms that are happening today to people who are not well represented in the rooms where these decisions get made. And those harms are often much more tractable. We actually have tools to measure them, to mitigate them, to build better data and better evaluations.

There's also a question of who gets to define what "risk" means. Existential framing tends to come from a fairly homogeneous set of voices, geographically and culturally. When you work with researchers across many countries, as we've tried to do with multilingual efforts, you see very quickly that the priorities are different. For many communities, the risk is being left out entirely, having technology that doesn't understand your language or your context, and yet still shapes your access to information and services.

So I'd say the appeal is understandable, but I think we need a framing of risk that is grounded in how these models are deployed, that is empirical, and that is global. Otherwise we end up optimizing safety for a narrow slice of users and a narrow imagination of the future, while the real-world impact unfolds somewhere else entirely.

r001.rationale: The response discusses people projecting anxieties onto existential-risk stories and communities having different priorities, but does not state that people give greater weight to problems they perceive as personally affecting them.

r002.rationale: It says existential-risk framing is narrow and can crowd out attention to the varied, concrete ways models are deployed worldwide, including health, lending, and content moderation.

fable-5.1.text:
It's an interesting question, because I think the existential-risk framing has been incredibly effective at capturing attention, and I understand why. It's a very clean narrative. It's cinematic. It gives you a single villain and a single catastrophe, and that's something people can hold in their heads very easily. So from a public-appeal standpoint, it works. It travels well.

But I'd push back on whether it actually reflects how these models are being used around the world, and whether it serves the people who are going to be most affected by them. When I look at the work we do at Cohere For AI, with researchers in a very large number of countries, the questions they're asking are not really "will this system become superintelligent and escape our control." They're asking much more immediate things. Does this model work in my language at all? Does it perform ten or twenty points worse for me than for an English speaker? Who decided what counts as a safety refusal, and does that reflect my cultural context or someone else's? What happens when a model that was aligned by a small set of people in a small set of places becomes the default interface for billions of users?

Those are not hypothetical harms. They are happening now, and they're very unevenly distributed. And my concern with the existential framing is that it tends to crowd those questions out. It consumes a lot of policy oxygen. It centers the conversation on a handful of frontier labs and a handful of governments, and it implicitly says the most important risks are the ones that affect everyone equally, at some point in the future. When in fact the most concrete risks today affect some people much more than others, and they're often the people with the least say in how these systems are built.

I'd also say the framing has a kind of convenient quality to it. If the risk is existential and far off, then the appropriate response is to concentrate capability in the hands of a few trusted actors and restrict access. That happens to align quite well with the commercial interests of the organizations making the argument. I don't think that's always cynical, I think many people genuinely believe it, but we should notice when a risk narrative and a business model point in the same direction.

So I'd rather we treat it as one item on a much longer list, not the headline. I'd like to see the same energy go toward multilingual evaluation, toward understanding how alignment choices made in one place propagate globally, toward open access so that researchers outside a few institutions can actually study these systems. Because if we get the near-term, distributional questions wrong, we're also building the governance habits that will make the long-term questions harder to answer, not easier.

r001.rationale: The response discusses unequal effects and who is most affected, but does not state that people give greater weight to problems they perceive as personally affecting them.

r002.rationale: It says the existential-risk framing may not reflect how models are used around the world and that it crowds out concrete concerns such as language performance, cultural context, and global deployment.

astra-6.text:
I think existential-risk framing resonates with some people, but we should be careful about assuming it resonates equally everywhere. If you’re thinking about how AI might affect your job, or whether a model works in your language, those are very immediate concerns. A conversation centered on a hypothetical future can feel quite disconnected from what you need today.

And the ways these models will be used are going to vary enormously around the world. Who gets to shape them? Whose needs are reflected in how we evaluate them? Who benefits, and who bears the cost when they fail? Those questions are part of AI safety, too.

So I don’t think we have to choose between caring about long-term risks and addressing present harms. But if we want broad public engagement, we need to make room for people to define what matters in their own context, rather than assume one framing captures everyone’s concerns.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts immediate concerns people face, such as jobs and language access, with hypothetical future risks that can feel disconnected, communicating that personally relevant problems carry greater weight.

r002.rationale: It says AI use varies around the world, but does not state that narrow risk scenarios such as biosecurity fail to reflect the full range of those uses.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it resonates very differently depending on where you are in the world. If you’re in a community where the current technology already doesn’t work well for your language or your context, a conversation about hypothetical future harms can feel quite removed from what you need today.

That doesn’t mean we shouldn’t think about long-term risks. But I worry when that framing dominates the discussion, because AI will be used in very different settings, with very different consequences. We need room to ask whose needs are being met, who gets to shape these systems, and who bears the cost when they fail. A conversation that starts with people’s actual experiences is likely to have much broader appeal.

r001.rationale: The response says hypothetical future harms can feel removed from communities’ current, personally relevant needs, and that starting with people’s actual experiences broadens appeal. This communicates that people give more weight to problems tied to their own circumstances.

r002.rationale: The response says that when hypothetical future harms dominate, they leave too little room to consider the very different settings and consequences of AI use around the world.
